3. The appellant herein as the pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.08 of 2001 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Narayanganj. His case, in short, is that he is a co-sharer with respondent Nos.2-10 and possessing the suit land in ejmali. The vendor-respondent Nos.2-10 surreptitiously sold the case land to respondent No.1 on 29.03.2000 without giving any notice to the pre-emptor-appellant. Respondent No.1 is a stranger to the case land and the pre-emptor-appellant came to know about the transfer of the case land on 12.02.2001 and hence the pre-emptor filed the above pre-emption miscellaneous case. 

 4. Pre-emptee-respondent No.1 contested the case by filing written objection denying all the material statements made in the pre-emption application of the case. His case, in short, is that pre-emptee-respondent Nos.2-10 expressed their willingness to sell the case land to co-sharer Abdul Aziz and to other co-sharers, who refused to purchase the case land. Finding no other alternative, the vendor approached the pre-emptee and the pre-emptee-respondent No.1 agreed to purchase the case land with the consent of the co-sharers including the pre-emptor. The pre-emptor filed the case after the statutory period of limitation seeing rapid increase of price of the landed property for illegal gain and the pre-emptee prayed for dismissal of the case with costs. 

 15. Admittedly, the appellant herein as the pre-emptor filed miscellaneous case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Narayanganj. The pre-emptor-appellant claimed that he is a co-sharer tenant by inheritance in the case holding with respondent Nos.2-10. The pre-emptor-appellant also claimed that vendor-respondent Nos.2-10 surreptitiously sold the case land to respondent No.1 on 29.03.2000 without giving any notice of transfer to him. The pre-emptor-appellant also claimed that respondent No.1 is a stranger to the case holding and that the pre-emptor came to know about the transfer of the case land on 12.02.2001 and filed the pre-emption case within the statutory period of limitation. 

 17. The pre-emptor-appellant in no uncertain terms stated that he is a co-sharer in the case holding by inheritance. The High Court Division for the reasons best known to it, on the other hand, considered the question of contiguous land ownership of the pre-emptor-appellant. This shows total non application of mind of the High Court Division in holding that the pre-emptor-appellant is not a contiguous land owner of all the plots transferred by the disputed deed of sale. 

 19. In order to substantiate its case of waiver and acquiescence, pre-emptee-respondent No.1 examined Md. Shohel Rana as O.P.W.1. While deposing before the Court on behalf of pre-emnptee-respondent No.1, this witness stated that before selling the case land to pre-emptee-respondent No.1, seller-respondent Nos.2- 10 informed about the sale to the co-sharers of the case holding. During cross-examination, he stated that he is not aware whether the pre-emptor-appellant refused to purchase the case land. The evidence of O.P.W.1 was not supported by any witness of the locality. 

 23. The principle expounded in the cases referred to above applies to the facts and circumstances of the case as the witness of the pre-emptee Shohel Rana deposed that before selling the case land, the pre-emptee-respondent and seller-respondent Nos.2 -10 informed the pre-emptor about the sale of the case land. He, however, during cross-examination, stated that he was not aware whether the pre-emptor-appellant refused to purchase the case land. Moreover, O.P.W.1 of the pre-emptee is an Accounts Officer of the pre-emptee-respondent and that no other witness was examined to prove the case of waiver and acquiescence. O.P.W.1 does not have any personal knowledge about the disputed sale under pre-emption as he was not a man of locality and as such, the pre-emptee-respondent had miserably failed to prove its case of waiver and acquiescence. 

 24. The pre-emptee-respondent claimed that it developed the case land by spending Tk. 500,000/- but O.P.W.1 stated in his cross-examination that filling-earth on the case land was not proved by any local investigation and that there is still water in the case land. Therefore, the pre-emptee-respondent failed to prove the case of improvement of the case land by spending Tk.500,000/-. The High Court Division erroneously came to the finding that the pre-emptee-respondent made improvement of the case land by spending Tk.500,000/-.
